completion.text:
Amid a summer marked by dangerous heat, drought, and floods, a new poll finds a clear majority of likely American voters now connect increasingly severe weather to the climate crisis — even as President Donald Trump continues to dismiss global heating as a "con job" and a "hoax," [according to the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study).

The survey, conducted by the progressive polling firm Data for Progress and shared exclusively with the Guardian, found that roughly six in ten likely voters — approximately 61% — hold that extreme weather events have grown more frequent over the preceding five years, [the Guardian reported](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study). That assessment crosses partisan lines: 72% of Democrats and 63% of Independents share it, along with nearly half of Republicans, at 46%.

When asked whether climate change is worsening specific categories of extreme weather, majorities attributed harm across multiple hazards. Wildfires drew the broadest connection at 64%, followed by droughts at 63%, [the Guardian reported](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study). Respondents placed flooding and flash flooding at 62%, while both hurricanes and severe thunderstorms or hailstorms each registered at 59%.

Heatwaves led all categories: 67% of respondents said climate change is making them worse, [according to the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study). That figure included 48% of Republicans — the highest Republican share recorded for any extreme weather type in the survey.

Grace Adcox, senior climate strategist at Data for Progress, suggested one reason heatwaves stand out: nearly everyone in the United States has experienced unusually hot days or weeks in recent years, she told the Guardian. The Guardian's reporting also cites the finding that high temperatures account for more annual deaths in the United States than hurricanes, tornadoes, and floods combined. Adcox said the heatwave result indicates that scorching conditions could serve as an "interesting opening salvo" for broader conversations about the climate crisis. "There are regional differences across experiences with extreme weather," she added, [according to the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study).

Adcox described the survey's framing as intentional. "We started with the question of our extreme weather events increasing, because we thought [that] if we can find consensus on that, that can be an entry point to being able to have a more bipartisan conversation about climate and climate intervention," [she told the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study). She also said the results suggest that political efforts to suppress or polarize climate concerns "may not be seeing full success."

Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island — who has long criticized fellow Democrats for muting their talk of global warming, a practice he calls "climate-hushing" — said the new data "adds to the mountain of evidence that the public is way ahead of the politicians on the dire consequences of climate change," [according to the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study). "Climate hushers who ignore this righteous fight should take note," Whitehouse told the Guardian.

Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, said the poll's findings are "very consistent" with conclusions from Yale's own surveys, which have shown Americans increasingly connecting extreme weather to the climate crisis and supporting worker heat protections, [the Guardian reported](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study).

Not all Yale researchers read the results as straightforwardly encouraging. Jennifer Marlon, a senior research scientist at Yale who focuses on climate communications, said it remains unclear whether most Americans understand the underlying cause of the changes they are observing, [according to the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study).
